newsitem.title: USA: Dow powers to 32nd record for year after election.
newsitem.headline: Dow powers to 32nd record for year after election.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average thundered Wednesday to its 32nd record of the year in a post-election rally as Wall Street bet that the status quo in Washington would keep stocks on their bullish track.
The Dow ended up 96.53 points at 6,177.71, eclipsing its old record of 6,094.23 set on Oct. 18.

"It looks like a post-election shopping spree," said Marty Kearney, a trader at PTI Securities. "There were no great surprises in the election and sidelined money wanted to go to work. With a long bond yield of 6.61 percent, people are going to stocks."
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks also set a record, jumping 10.45 points to 724.59. The NYSE Composite index rose 5.12 to 383.55, also a record.
It was the Dow's first-ever close above 6,100 and its biggest single day point gain since March 18, when it closed up 98.63 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,701 to 756 on heavy volume of 509 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Democrat President Clinton easily turned back Republican challenger Bob Dole on Tuesday, but the GOP held its small majorities in both houses of Congress, setting the stage for continuing moderation in fiscal policy.
"The market is happy with the fact there are no big changes. It's status quo," said Richard McCabe, chief technical analyst at Merrill Lynch.
As for the near term, McCabe said, "We may get to 6,200 or 6,300 and then people will take a look."
"My concern is we may be in a later stage or mature stage of the bull market," he said. "If the market stalls at year end or early next year, there could be a sizeable 20 percent pullback in 1997."
Analysts said the stock market was still viewed as the best place for investors to place their money.
"We go back to last year's argument that there's no alternative to stocks with yields this low," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slipped 13/32 and its yield was edged up to 6.62 percent from 6.59 percent on Tuesday.

Drug, health care, and tobacco shares surged on investor perception that a Republican Congress will keep a second Clinton administration from launching any aggressive campaigns to regulate the industries.

Merck rose 3-1/4 to 79, Pfizer was up 2-7/8 to 88-1/2 and Bristol-Myers Squibb gained 2-1/2 to 111. United Healthcare jumped 2-3/4 to 40 while Oxford Health Plans, which also posted strong third quarter earnings, rose 4-5/8 to 51-1/2.
Among biotech shares, Biogen rose 3-3/8 to 77-1/8 and Centocor climbed 2-5/8 to 29.
Philip Morris rose 3-7/8 to 97-3/8, RJR Nabisco gained 1 to 30-1/8 and Loews added 2-5/8 to 85.
Technology stocks, particularily those based in California, rose after the state's voters defeated a ballot measure that would have reduced obstacles to filing shareholder lawsuits.
Intel surged 4-7/8 to 118-7/8. After the close, Intel forecast its fourth-quarter revenues would be significantly above the third quarter's levels. Intel soared to 120 in after-hours trading.
Hewlett-Packard rose 1-1/4 to 45-3/8, and Advanced Micro Devices gained 5/8 to 19-3/4.
Meadowbrook Insurance slumped 10-7/8 to 15-1/2 after reporting sharply lower quarterly results.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 16.42 points to 1,245.49. The American Stock Exchange index rose 4.25 to 577.87.
The average NYSE share was up 54 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at a record 7,013.896 up 93.611 or 1.35 percent.
